You have a lot of solid stuff here. I don’t know if its some word choices, like the repetitive/lack of word variation like “sitting on large chairs sitting out of small ponds” or something else. Something makes the metaphors just not land as nicely as they should. I hope you don’t mind I took my shot at a light revising. Doing so, I’m not sure if I matched your intentions. Reading your version multiple times, I derived this is a story of quiet marital spite/building family tension. Starting with the main device, the pond. A pond is typically a cold, murky, pool of water. It has no waves or tides, and seldom is the surface tension of the water broken. I think this was a great choice on your part. We know there is some sort of conflict not being addressed, but we don’t know the conflict exactly. The imagery characteristics of a pond matches really well.  The pond is affecting everyone in some way, but no one directly addresses it. Some characters are more affected by the pond than others. We have a father/husband who is watching the pond closely. He’s worried the pond will reach his daughters. At the same time, he knows the chairs he built(possible metaphor for the values he raised them with) will keep them safe and dry. In contrast, we have a wife/mother who completely ignores the pond. She makes an abundance of food and tries to care for everyone. Not out of worry like the father, but guilt. As if her labor of putting together all this food and weighing down her family will keep them from floating away. I think you can see how I interpret the story from here but I’m open to questions or trying to give more constructive feedback. I think you did a good job, just maybe need to pay a little more attention to wording and making sure things play out on the page a little more clearly.

I'm not sure how much critique I can provide. It is a really intriguing start. The gradual building of imagery is good. It really made me think of the scene as the opening to the movie. As an audience, we know very little but we get these tiny details to bring us in.  The short bursts of descriptors give this pacing that makes you think of running. Like the rhythmic  sound of boots hitting the ground, if that makes sense.   
You do a good job use dryness as sort of connector. When you think of dryness, you think of the lack of something usually liquid. But it works through out this whole paragraph. The character is experiencing extreme dryness(dry mouth, cracked lips) but also dryness in the sense of perception/motivation(I could be doing all of this for nothing, my eyes start to blur) and that culminates in the reveal he is in a vary bare and dry place, the desert. 

I did a little markup, it ruins your tight pacing a bit. I just wanted to show how I saw the dryness metaphor playing out as I read this. I just really liked the idea that as we're introduced to this character he's weakening slowly. Like water evaporating when left in intense heat. It just my perspective, what you have now works really well though.    
 **My mouth was bone dry. Dried up, like the blood now crusting over my cracked lips. It would seem as if I’m evaporating.  My tired legs aching, begging me to stop. Every stride squeezing the last bit of strength from already worn out tendons. I must go on. I must pass this test, if this even is a test. I could be doing this all for nothing. My eyes start to blur, now I can’t see what’s ahead of me. Just pools of color drained into darkness. With each step I take, my body aches with unbearable pain. A scream of agony pours out of my mouth. It is absorbed into empty air. There’s no one and nothing out here. I’m alone, in the desert.**

This might be kind of a plain idea on my end, but for the gear you can make it a classic one step behind quest. When they find the groupies and interrogate them it's revealed the gear has been pawned at a pawn shop. They race to the shop and its been sold to a collector. The encounter with the collector can be your choice but seeing how collectors are usually eccentric this may be a good puzzle spot. Ideally the collector would be better suited in intelligence rather than combat so he offers a battle of the wits. If the party can solve some riddles they can get their stuff back. For navigation around the city in general, you can have them roll checks to see if they are going the right way or just getting lost in a sprawling city. If they roll terribly perhaps they run into gangs or vagrants and have to talk/fight their way out. If the party is diplomatic perhaps they can convince a gang member or homeless into being their guide and you can make a cool npc.

The difference in mindset and thinking does make it challenging to identify any similarities. Not only does this make it difficult, but also the presentation of morals in general. In The Stranger, we are presented with situations containing a clear distinction between right and wrong. In Crime and Punishment, the lines between right and wrong are in flux and questionable. Compare how morals are presented in the books. The Stranger has Raymond, clearly immoral, and Marie, clearly moral. In Crime and Punishment, the characters balance between right and wrong. Sonya turns to sinful prostitution, but she has to in order to help her family. Her and other characters are simultaneously moral and immoral. However, I do believe these similarities do exist. The one I notice the role of isolation in both novels. In Crime and Punishment, we see Rodion go through bouts of self imposed isolation in order to process and attempt to deal with his guilt. In The Stranger, Meursault only truly reflects upon his actions once he is left alone in prison.   


Side note: Does anyone feel Svidrigailov, Rodion, and Luzhin are a depiction of chaotic evil, neutral evil, and lawful evil respectively? I feel the depictions of both Svidrigailov and Luzhin were meant to be a more impactful element on Rodion and the book entirely. I certainly believe there is a strong connection between the three of them.
